question.text: Unless posted otherwise, what is the New Jersey speed limit in school zones and in business or residential districts?

answer.text: Unless another limit is posted, the New Jersey speed limit is twenty-five miles per hour in school zones and in business or residential districts.

teaching.text: The word suburban is what separates this limit from the next one up, so without it, think of the lower number. Remember: School and town: twenty-five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unless another limit is posted, the New Jersey speed limit is twenty-five miles per hour in school zones and in business or residential districts.

question.text: Unless posted otherwise, what is the limit in suburban business and residential districts?

answer.text: Unless another limit is posted, the limit in suburban business and residential districts is thirty-five miles per hour

teaching.text: Suburban is the key word here; drop it and the default falls to the lower town limit. Remember: Suburbs get thirty-five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unless another limit is posted, the limit in suburban business and residential districts is thirty-five miles per hour

question.text: Which two low default limits are easy to swap, and which places does each cover?

answer.text: The two lowest default limits are easy to swap: twenty-five miles per hour covers school zones and business or residential districts, while thirty-five miles per hour covers suburban business and residential districts.

teaching.text: Tie twenty-five to school and town districts, and thirty-five to the word suburban. Remember: Town twenty-five, suburb thirty-five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The two lowest default limits are easy to swap: twenty-five miles per hour covers school zones and business or residential districts, while thirty-five miles per hour covers suburban business and residential districts.

question.text: Unless posted otherwise, what is the limit on rural roads without posted limits?

answer.text: Unless another limit is posted, the limit on rural roads without posted limits is fifty miles per hour

teaching.text: This default covers open country roads that have no posted limit, a step above the suburban default. Remember: Rural roads run fifty.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unless another limit is posted, the limit on rural roads without posted limits is fifty miles per hour

question.text: Where does the fifty-five miles per hour limit apply?

answer.text: The fifty-five miles per hour limit applies to certain state highways, as posted, and to interstates.

teaching.text: This is the limit tied to certain posted state highways and to interstates in general, one step below the top. Remember: Fifty-five: state highways, interstates.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The fifty-five miles per hour limit applies to certain state highways, as posted, and to interstates.

question.text: Where does the sixty-five miles per hour limit apply?

answer.text: The sixty-five miles per hour limit applies only to certain interstate highways where it is posted.

teaching.text: The word only matters: this limit is never assumed, it must be posted on certain interstates. Remember: Sixty-five only where posted.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The sixty-five miles per hour limit applies only to certain interstate highways where it is posted.

question.text: Which two highway limits are easy to swap, and where does each apply?

answer.text: The two highway limits are also easy to swap: fifty-five miles per hour applies to certain posted state highways and to interstates, while sixty-five miles per hour applies only to certain posted interstate highways.

teaching.text: Tie fifty-five to posted state highways and interstates, and sixty-five only to posted interstates. Remember: State fifty-five, posted sixty-five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The two highway limits are also easy to swap: fifty-five miles per hour applies to certain posted state highways and to interstates, while sixty-five miles per hour applies only to certain posted interstate highways.

question.text: What happens to fines when you speed well over the limit in a sixty-five miles per hour zone?

answer.text: Going ten miles per hour or more over the sixty-five miles per hour limit doubles the fine, and most other moving violations in a sixty-five miles per hour zone carry doubled fines too.

teaching.text: The top of the speed ladder carries the top penalty, and the doubling reaches most other moving violations in that zone as well. Remember: Sixty-five zone, double trouble.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Going ten miles per hour or more over the sixty-five miles per hour limit doubles the fine, and most other moving violations in a sixty-five miles per hour zone carry doubled fines too.

question.text: How does speeding change your crash risk and your ability to respond?

answer.text: Speeding raises both the chance of a crash and how severe it is, and it leaves the driver less time to react to hazards or correct mistakes.

teaching.text: Speed works against you twice: crashes become likelier and worse, and you lose the time you would need to fix a mistake. Remember: Faster means harder, sooner crashes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Speeding raises both the chance of a crash and how severe it is, and it leaves the driver less time to react to hazards or correct mistakes.

question.text: How does a small increase in speed affect a pedestrian struck in a crash?

answer.text: Even a small increase in speed sharply raises the risk that a pedestrian struck in a crash is badly hurt or killed, and lower speeds greatly improve pedestrian survival.

teaching.text: A pedestrian has no protection, so even a few extra miles per hour can decide whether they survive. Remember: Slower saves walkers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Even a small increase in speed sharply raises the risk that a pedestrian struck in a crash is badly hurt or killed, and lower speeds greatly improve pedestrian survival.

question.text: Can you always drive at the posted limit, whatever the weather, road or traffic?

answer.text: Never drive faster than the weather, road or traffic allows, whatever the posted limit says; driving too fast for conditions can bring a moving violation.

teaching.text: The sign gives an upper bound, not a promise; the weather, the road and the traffic can all set a lower safe speed. Remember: Conditions outrank the sign.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive faster than the weather, road or traffic allows, whatever the posted limit says; driving too fast for conditions can bring a moving violation.

question.text: In which places and conditions should you always slow down?

answer.text: Always slow down on narrow or winding roads, at intersections and railroad crossings, on hills, at sharp or blind curves, near pedestrians or hazards, on wet or icy roads and when visibility is limited.

teaching.text: Each place on the list hides something or shortens your grip, from a blind curve to an icy road, so speed comes down there. Remember: Narrow, hilly, wet: ease off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always slow down on narrow or winding roads, at intersections and railroad crossings, on hills, at sharp or blind curves, near pedestrians or hazards, on wet or icy roads and when visibility is limited.

question.text: How should you enter a curve?

answer.text: Enter a curve by slowing down beforehand and staying out of other lanes, and watch for vehicles drifting into yours.

teaching.text: The slowing happens before the curve, so you can stay in your lane through it. Remember: Slow before the bend.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Enter a curve by slowing down beforehand and staying out of other lanes, and watch for vehicles drifting into yours.

question.text: When the road and traffic are normal, what does New Jersey law say about driving too slowly?

answer.text: When the road surface and traffic are normal, New Jersey law forbids holding up traffic by driving too slowly.

teaching.text: The rule cuts both ways: in normal conditions, holding up traffic by crawling is also against the law. Remember: Crawling holds everyone up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When the road surface and traffic are normal, New Jersey law forbids holding up traffic by driving too slowly.

question.text: Can driving too slowly cause crashes, and what do you do if your vehicle cannot keep up?

answer.text: Some crashes are caused by driving too slowly or backing up in traffic; if a vehicle problem keeps you from keeping up, pull safely off the road and turn on the hazard lights.

teaching.text: Driving too slowly can cause crashes too, so a car that cannot keep up belongs off the road with hazards on. Remember: Too slow? Pull off, hazards.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Some crashes are caused by driving too slowly or backing up in traffic; if a vehicle problem keeps you from keeping up, pull safely off the road and turn on the hazard lights.

question.text: What does it mean for passing when both center lines are solid?

answer.text: When both center lines are solid, no passing is allowed.

teaching.text: Two solid lines work like two walls, so neither driver may move into the oncoming lane to pass. Remember: Double solid, stay put.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When both center lines are solid, no passing is allowed.

question.text: When one center line is broken and the other solid, who may pass?

answer.text: When one center line is broken, passing is allowed only from the side with the broken line.

teaching.text: Only the driver who sees the broken line on their own side may pass; the solid side stays put. Remember: Broken on your side, go.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When one center line is broken, passing is allowed only from the side with the broken line.

question.text: When both center lines are broken, from which side may you pass?

answer.text: When both center lines are broken, passing is allowed from either side.

teaching.text: Two broken lines open the door from both directions, though each driver still needs a safe gap. Remember: Double broken, both may pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When both center lines are broken, passing is allowed from either side.

question.text: How do you read center line markings for passing?

answer.text: Center line markings read from your own side: two solid lines forbid passing, a broken line on your side permits it, and two broken lines permit it from both sides.

teaching.text: Only the line on your own side tells you whether you may pass. Remember: Read lines from your side.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Center line markings read from your own side: two solid lines forbid passing, a broken line on your side permits it, and two broken lines permit it from both sides.

question.text: By when must every pass be finished?

answer.text: Every pass must be finished before the center lines turn solid again.

teaching.text: A pass that starts legally must also end legally, so if the solid line is coming soon, do not begin. Remember: Done before the solid.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Every pass must be finished before the center lines turn solid again.

question.text: Can solid no-passing lines ever be crossed, and if so when?

answer.text: Solid lines between intersections mark no-passing zones, but they may be crossed carefully when turning into or out of a driveway in a business or residential area.

teaching.text: Solid lines ban passing, not driveway turns, which may cross them with care in business or residential areas. Remember: Driveways may cross solid.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Solid lines between intersections mark no-passing zones, but they may be crossed carefully when turning into or out of a driveway in a business or residential area.

question.text: What does the Safe Corridors law do on designated state highways?

answer.text: The Safe Corridors law, signed in July two thousand three, doubles fines on designated state highways for offenses such as speeding and aggressive driving.

teaching.text: Where crashes cluster on designated state highways, offenses such as speeding and aggressive driving cost twice as much. Remember: Safe Corridors, double fines.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The Safe Corridors law, signed in July two thousand three, doubles fines on designated state highways for offenses such as speeding and aggressive driving.

question.text: When is a highway designated a Safe Corridor?

answer.text: Highways are designated Safe Corridors when their crash rate is fifty percent above the state rate and at least one thousand crashes were reported over three years.

teaching.text: Designation is earned by crash numbers: a high crash rate and many reported crashes over three years. Remember: High crash rate earns designation.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Highways are designated Safe Corridors when their crash rate is fifty percent above the state rate and at least one thousand crashes were reported over three years.

question.text: On which side do you normally pass, and when is passing on the right permitted?

answer.text: Passing is normally done on the left; passing on the right is permitted only where the road has more than one lane in your direction and traffic is moving in two or more steady lines, or where the driver ahead is turning left and there is room.

teaching.text: The left is the normal passing side, and the right opens only in steady multi-lane traffic or beside a driver turning left with room. Remember: Left normally, right rarely.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing is normally done on the left; passing on the right is permitted only where the road has more than one lane in your direction and traffic is moving in two or more steady lines, or where the driver ahead is turning left and there is room.

question.text: Is passing on the right shoulder of the road ever allowed?

answer.text: Passing on the right shoulder of the road is never allowed and is against the law.

teaching.text: The shoulder is never a passing lane, even in a jam or beside a driver turning left. Remember: Shoulder is never a lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing on the right shoulder of the road is never allowed and is against the law.

question.text: In which places must you not pass another vehicle?

answer.text: Do not pass on a hill or curve or whenever you cannot see far enough ahead, at an intersection or railroad crossing, on narrow bridges or in underpasses or tunnels, where signs or center lines forbid it, or behind a vehicle stopped to let a pedestrian cross.

teaching.text: Every place on the list is somewhere you might not see trouble in time, such as a hill, a tunnel or a car stopped for a walker. Remember: Can't see? Don't pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not pass on a hill or curve or whenever you cannot see far enough ahead, at an intersection or railroad crossing, on narrow bridges or in underpasses or tunnels, where signs or center lines forbid it, or behind a vehicle stopped to let a pedestrian cross.

question.text: Which part of the road does New Jersey law require you to drive on?

answer.text: New Jersey law requires driving on the right half of the road, as close as practical to the right edge or curb, except when passing or on a one-way street.

teaching.text: Keeping right leaves the left half for passing and for oncoming traffic, unless you are on a one-way street. Remember: Hug the right half.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: New Jersey law requires driving on the right half of the road, as close as practical to the right edge or curb, except when passing or on a one-way street.

question.text: On a multi-lane road, which lane should you use?

answer.text: On a multi-lane road, use the available lane nearest the right edge or curb, except when overtaking another vehicle or preparing for a left turn.

teaching.text: The rightmost available lane is the default, and you leave it only to overtake or to set up a left turn. Remember: Rightmost lane by default.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a multi-lane road, use the available lane nearest the right edge or curb, except when overtaking another vehicle or preparing for a left turn.

question.text: Which vehicles must you always yield to?

answer.text: Always yield to police cars, fire engines and ambulances that are using sirens or flashing lights, and to a train approaching a railroad crossing.

teaching.text: Sirens, flashing lights and an approaching train always win the right-of-way, so you give way every time. Remember: Sirens, lights and trains win.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always yield to police cars, fire engines and ambulances that are using sirens or flashing lights, and to a train approaching a railroad crossing.

question.text: Which vehicles re-entering the flow of traffic get the right-of-way?

answer.text: Buses and postal vehicles re-entering the flow of traffic are given the right-of-way.

teaching.text: Buses and postal vehicles pulling back into traffic are given the way, so let them merge. Remember: Buses and mail trucks merge.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Buses and postal vehicles re-entering the flow of traffic are given the right-of-way.

question.text: Must a crosswalk be painted, and where do crosswalks exist?

answer.text: Crosswalks may be marked or unmarked, and one exists at every corner of an intersection unless signs prohibit pedestrians from crossing there.

teaching.text: Paint does not create a crosswalk; every corner has one unless signs prohibit crossing there. Remember: Every corner has one.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Crosswalks may be marked or unmarked, and one exists at every corner of an intersection unless signs prohibit pedestrians from crossing there.

question.text: What must a driver do for a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk or at an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection?

answer.text: A driver must come to a full stop, not merely slow or yield, for a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk or one crossing at an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection.

teaching.text: Slowing or yielding is not enough here; the wheels must stop, at painted and unpainted crosswalks alike. Remember: Full stop, not a slow roll.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver must come to a full stop, not merely slow or yield, for a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk or one crossing at an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Full stop, not a slow roll

question.text: After stopping for a pedestrian, how long must you stay stopped?

answer.text: Stay stopped until the pedestrian has cleared both your lane and the next lane going in your direction.

teaching.text: The person may still be in front of the driver next to you, so you wait until two lanes are clear. Remember: Two lanes clear, then go.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay stopped until the pedestrian has cleared both your lane and the next lane going in your direction.

question.text: If the signal changes to Don't Walk while a pedestrian is still in the crosswalk, what do you do?

answer.text: Stop for every pedestrian still in a crosswalk even if the signal has changed to Don't Walk.

teaching.text: A changing signal does not move the pedestrian, so anyone still in the crosswalk still gets your stop. Remember: Signal changed? Still stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stop for every pedestrian still in a crosswalk even if the signal has changed to Don't Walk.

question.text: What two things must you never do around a crosswalk?

answer.text: Never overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian, and never block or park in a crosswalk.

teaching.text: The stopped car may be hiding a pedestrian you cannot see, which is why going around it is never allowed. Remember: Never pass the stopped car.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian, and never block or park in a crosswalk.

question.text: What penalties can a driver face for not stopping for a pedestrian?

answer.text: Not stopping for a pedestrian can cost a fine of up to five hundred, dollars a jail term of up to twenty-five days, community service, a suspension of driving privileges of up to six months, and two motor vehicle points.

teaching.text: One missed stop can bring several penalties at once: a fine, jail, community service, suspension and points. Remember: Fine, jail, suspension, points.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Not stopping for a pedestrian can cost a fine of up to five hundred, dollars a jail term of up to twenty-five days, community service, a suspension of driving privileges of up to six months, and two motor vehicle points.

question.text: Besides walkers, who else must you yield to at crosswalks and intersections?

answer.text: Yield to people using motorized or mobility-assistance devices in a crosswalk or trying to cross, and to other vehicles already inside the intersection.

teaching.text: Anyone crossing slowly with a mobility device gets the same yield as a walker, as do vehicles already in the intersection. Remember: Mobility devices get way too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Yield to people using motorized or mobility-assistance devices in a crosswalk or trying to cross, and to other vehicles already inside the intersection.

question.text: Where do most crashes happen, and what does a single solid white line across the road there mean?

answer.text: Most crashes happen at intersections, and a single solid white line across the road there means stopping behind it for a traffic signal or sign.

teaching.text: Since most crashes happen at intersections, the white line shows exactly where your car should wait. Remember: White line: stop behind it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most crashes happen at intersections, and a single solid white line across the road there means stopping behind it for a traffic signal or sign.

question.text: Is cutting through private property to avoid a traffic signal or sign allowed?

answer.text: Cutting through private property to get around a traffic signal or sign is a motor vehicle violation.

teaching.text: Driving around a signal or sign through private property does not avoid the rule; it breaks it. Remember: No shortcut around signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Cutting through private property to get around a traffic signal or sign is a motor vehicle violation.

question.text: At a multi-way stop, who goes first when two drivers arrive at the same moment?

answer.text: At a multi-way stop, a driver who arrives at the same moment as another yields to the one on the right, and also yields to any vehicle already stopped there.

teaching.text: A tie goes to the driver on the right, and anyone already stopped goes before you. Remember: Tie at stop? Right goes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a multi-way stop, a driver who arrives at the same moment as another yields to the one on the right, and also yields to any vehicle already stopped there.

question.text: What must you do at a yield sign?

answer.text: At a yield sign, slow down and give the right-of-way to traffic on the crossing road, stopping if needed.

teaching.text: Yield means give way, not always stop; you stop only when crossing traffic needs the space. Remember: Yield means slow and give.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a yield sign, slow down and give the right-of-way to traffic on the crossing road, stopping if needed.

question.text: How does the multi-way stop rule differ from the yield sign rule?

answer.text: A multi-way stop gives the right-of-way to the driver on the right when two arrive together, while a yield sign requires slowing and giving way to the crossing road's traffic.

teaching.text: A stop always means stopping and a tie goes right, while a yield means giving way and stopping only if needed. Remember: Stop ties go right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A multi-way stop gives the right-of-way to the driver on the right when two arrive together, while a yield sign requires slowing and giving way to the crossing road's traffic.

question.text: At a stop sign, where must you stop and when may you go on?

answer.text: At a stop sign, come to a complete stop within five feet of the nearest crosswalk or stop line, then enter only after yielding to pedestrians and to any traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard.

teaching.text: The stop is required every time and close to the line, then you yield before entering. Remember: Stop close, then yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a stop sign, come to a complete stop within five feet of the nearest crosswalk or stop line, then enter only after yielding to pedestrians and to any traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard.

question.text: How do you treat a traffic signal that is dark because of a power failure?

answer.text: A traffic signal that is dark because of a power failure or other malfunction is treated as a four-way stop.

teaching.text: A dark signal turns the intersection into a stop for everyone, and the multi-way stop rules then apply. Remember: Dark light, four-way stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A traffic signal that is dark because of a power failure or other malfunction is treated as a four-way stop.

question.text: How do you approach an uncontrolled crossroad, and what do you do coming out of a driveway?

answer.text: Approaching an uncontrolled crossroad, slow down and be ready to stop for traffic from either side, and when coming out of a private road or driveway yield to all traffic on the main road.

teaching.text: Without signs, you slow for both sides, and leaving a driveway means everyone on the main road goes first. Remember: Driveway drivers yield to all.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Approaching an uncontrolled crossroad, slow down and be ready to stop for traffic from either side, and when coming out of a private road or driveway yield to all traffic on the main road.

question.text: What can block your view of cross traffic, and what should you do about it?

answer.text: On rural roads trees or crops, and elsewhere buildings, parked cars or bushes, can block the view of cross traffic, so slow down or stop fully before going ahead.

teaching.text: When crops, trees, buildings or parked cars hide cross traffic, slowing or stopping fully buys you the view you lack. Remember: Can't see across? Slow down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On rural roads trees or crops, and elsewhere buildings, parked cars or bushes, can block the view of cross traffic, so slow down or stop fully before going ahead.

question.text: As a general rule at an uncontrolled intersection, which vehicle yields?

answer.text: As a general rule at an uncontrolled intersection, the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle on the right.

teaching.text: This general rule is the backstop whenever no sign or signal decides who goes. Remember: Left yields to right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: As a general rule at an uncontrolled intersection, the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle on the right.

question.text: What decides the right-of-way in a New Jersey traffic circle?

answer.text: New Jersey has no set rules for traffic circles: the circle's established flow pattern usually decides the right-of-way, a major highway running through it usually dominates, and stop or yield signs at the entrances also govern.

teaching.text: With no set rules, you read the clues: the flow, a major highway through the circle, and the entrance signs. Remember: Circles follow the flow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: New Jersey has no set rules for traffic circles: the circle's established flow pattern usually decides the right-of-way, a major highway running through it usually dominates, and stop or yield signs at the entrances also govern.

question.text: When right-of-way in a traffic circle is unclear, what rule do you fall back on?

answer.text: When it is unclear who has the right-of-way in a traffic circle, fall back on the basic uncontrolled-intersection rule: the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle approaching from the right.

teaching.text: When a circle leaves it unclear, the ordinary crossroad rule takes over: left yields to right. Remember: Unsure in circle? Right wins.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When it is unclear who has the right-of-way in a traffic circle, fall back on the basic uncontrolled-intersection rule: the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle approaching from the right.

question.text: What are highways, parkways and turnpikes like, and who yields when you enter them?

answer.text: Highways, parkways and turnpikes are divided roads with speeds up to sixty-five miles per hour and no direct intersections, entered by an acceleration lane, and drivers must yield to traffic already on the main road.

teaching.text: These roads have no direct intersections, so entering by the acceleration lane and yielding to main road traffic is how you join. Remember: Main road traffic has priority.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Highways, parkways and turnpikes are divided roads with speeds up to sixty-five miles per hour and no direct intersections, entered by an acceleration lane, and drivers must yield to traffic already on the main road.

question.text: What should you do as you leave the acceleration lane to enter a highway?

answer.text: When entering a highway, speed up to the flow of traffic as you leave the acceleration lane and avoid stopping completely in that lane.

teaching.text: Merging at the speed of traffic is far easier than merging from a standstill, so keep rolling. Remember: Match the flow, keep rolling.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When entering a highway, speed up to the flow of traffic as you leave the acceleration lane and avoid stopping completely in that lane.

question.text: What should you do if you miss your highway exit?

answer.text: If you miss an exit, continue to the next one, and never back up on an exit ramp or deceleration lane.

teaching.text: Missing an exit costs only time, while backing up on a ramp risks a crash, so take the next one. Remember: Missed it? Take the next.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you miss an exit, continue to the next one, and never back up on an exit ramp or deceleration lane.

question.text: How does an acceleration lane differ from a deceleration lane?

answer.text: An acceleration lane is for speeding up and should not be stopped in, while a deceleration lane is where you start slowing down and obey its advisory speed.

teaching.text: The acceleration lane is for gaining speed and the deceleration lane is for losing it; never mix them up. Remember: Speed up there, slow here.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An acceleration lane is for speeding up and should not be stopped in, while a deceleration lane is where you start slowing down and obey its advisory speed.

question.text: On which side are most exit ramps, and what do you do when an exit is on the left?

answer.text: Most exit ramps and deceleration lanes are on the right; when an exit is on the left, follow the signs that direct traffic to the proper exit lane.

teaching.text: Exits usually sit on the right, so a left exit needs you to follow its signs into the proper lane early. Remember: Exits mostly right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most exit ramps and deceleration lanes are on the right; when an exit is on the left, follow the signs that direct traffic to the proper exit lane.

question.text: In a weave lane, which driver must yield?

answer.text: In a weave lane, which serves as both an entrance and an exit, the driver coming from the entrance ramp must yield to the driver leaving the expressway.

teaching.text: The exiting driver is already on the expressway, so the driver coming from the ramp yields. Remember: Leaving beats entering.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a weave lane, which serves as both an entrance and an exit, the driver coming from the entrance ramp must yield to the driver leaving the expressway.

question.text: How should you drive through a cloverleaf interchange?

answer.text: At a cloverleaf interchange, watch for the entrance and exit signs and drive slowly through the loop at the posted speed.

teaching.text: Cloverleaf loops are tight, so you follow the signs and keep to the posted speed. Remember: Loop slowly at posted speed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a cloverleaf interchange, watch for the entrance and exit signs and drive slowly through the loop at the posted speed.

question.text: During rush hour on highways through cities, which lanes should you use?

answer.text: On highways through cities, drive in the left or center lane during rush hour to avoid merge conflicts, and look for your exit early.

teaching.text: The right lanes of a city highway are where merging traffic meets, so at rush hour stay left or center. Remember: Rush hour: left or center.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On highways through cities, drive in the left or center lane during rush hour to avoid merge conflicts, and look for your exit early.

question.text: How should you approach and leave a toll plaza?

answer.text: At toll plazas, slow down early because traffic may back up, look for green lights marking open booths, and check both sides for merging traffic when leaving.

teaching.text: Traffic may back up before the booths, and merging cars may come from both sides after them. Remember: Green light, open booth.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At toll plazas, slow down early because traffic may back up, look for green lights marking open booths, and check both sides for merging traffic when leaving.

question.text: What should you do when you see a disabled vehicle ahead?

answer.text: When you see a disabled vehicle ahead, slow down and leave more space, possibly by changing lanes, and watch for pedestrians, tow trucks and police.

teaching.text: People, tow trucks and police may be near a disabled car, so you slow and give extra room. Remember: Slow and give space.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you see a disabled vehicle ahead, slow down and leave more space, possibly by changing lanes, and watch for pedestrians, tow trucks and police.

question.text: What should you do if your vehicle breaks down on the road?

answer.text: If your vehicle breaks down, pull as far onto the shoulder or median as you can, turn on the flashers, raise the hood, stay inside with the seat belt on and doors locked, and never get into a stranger's vehicle.

teaching.text: Staying inside, buckled and locked, is the safest way to wait, and a stranger's vehicle is never the answer. Remember: Pull off, flash, stay locked.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your vehicle breaks down, pull as far onto the shoulder or median as you can, turn on the flashers, raise the hood, stay inside with the seat belt on and doors locked, and never get into a stranger's vehicle.

question.text: When turning left, who must you yield to and stop for?

answer.text: When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic and stop for pedestrians in the crosswalk.

teaching.text: A left turn crosses the path of oncoming cars and walkers, so they go first. Remember: Left turn waits for oncoming.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic and stop for pedestrians in the crosswalk.

question.text: What should you check before any turn, including a right turn on red?

answer.text: Watch carefully for pedestrians when turning, including right turns on red, and before any turn scan left, right and behind and check mirrors and blind spots for cyclists and pedestrians.

teaching.text: A careful scan of every direction and your blind spots catches the cyclist or walker you might otherwise miss. Remember: Scan, mirrors, blind spots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Watch carefully for pedestrians when turning, including right turns on red, and before any turn scan left, right and behind and check mirrors and blind spots for cyclists and pedestrians.

question.text: When may you turn right on a red light, and who must you yield to first?

answer.text: Unless a No Turn on Red sign is posted, a right turn on red is allowed after a full stop, and the driver must yield to all oncoming traffic and pedestrians first.

teaching.text: Turning on red needs three things: no sign against it, a full stop, and yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. Remember: Stop, yield, then right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unless a No Turn on Red sign is posted, a right turn on red is allowed after a full stop, and the driver must yield to all oncoming traffic and pedestrians first.

question.text: What might be moving while you turn right on red?

answer.text: Bicycles, mopeds and other hard-to-see vehicles may have a green light while you turn right on red, so look for them before turning.

teaching.text: A red light for you can mean a green light for a bike or moped, so look before turning. Remember: Bikes may have green.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicycles, mopeds and other hard-to-see vehicles may have a green light while you turn right on red, so look for them before turning.

question.text: How should you position your vehicle for a right turn?

answer.text: For a right turn, approach as far to the right as possible, close to the curb or parked cars, and do not swing wide or into another lane.

teaching.text: Staying tight to the right closes the gap where a cyclist or another car could slip in. Remember: Tight to the curb.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a right turn, approach as far to the right as possible, close to the curb or parked cars, and do not swing wide or into another lane.

question.text: When two vehicles facing each other both turn left, how should each turn?

answer.text: When two vehicles facing each other both turn left, each should turn to the left of the center of the intersection when it is safe.

teaching.text: Each driver turns to the left of the center point, so both can complete the turn when it is safe. Remember: Pass left of center.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When two vehicles facing each other both turn left, each should turn to the left of the center of the intersection when it is safe.

question.text: For a left turn from a one-way road onto another one-way road, which lanes do you use?

answer.text: For a left turn from a one-way road onto another one-way road, approach in the left lane and turn into the left lane of the new road.

teaching.text: Between one-way roads, a left turn stays on the left from start to finish. Remember: Left lane to left lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a left turn from a one-way road onto another one-way road, approach in the left lane and turn into the left lane of the new road.

question.text: For a left turn from a two-way road onto a four-lane highway, which lane do you turn into?

answer.text: For a left turn from a two-way road onto a four-lane highway, turn into the lane nearest the center line, which is the passing lane, and move right out of it when traffic allows.

teaching.text: The lane nearest the center line is the passing lane, so you use it to arrive and then move right. Remember: Center-side lane, then move right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a left turn from a two-way road onto a four-lane highway, turn into the lane nearest the center line, which is the passing lane, and move right out of it when traffic allows.

question.text: For a left turn from a two-way road onto another two-way road, how do you approach and where do you end up?

answer.text: For a left turn from a two-way road onto another two-way road, approach close to the line nearest the center of the road and keep to the right of the center line of the road you enter.

teaching.text: Ending right of the new center line is the two-way rule; the four-lane turn uses the passing lane instead. Remember: Stay right of new center.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a left turn from a two-way road onto another two-way road, approach close to the line nearest the center of the road and keep to the right of the center line of the road you enter.

hooks_spoken: Unless signs say otherwise, think twenty-five in school zones and towns, thirty-five in the suburbs, and fifty on unposted rural roads.
Fifty-five covers certain posted state highways and interstates, sixty-five only certain posted interstates, and ten or more over sixty-five doubles the fine.

hooks_spoken: Speed makes crashes likelier and worse, hits pedestrians hardest, and the posted limit never outranks weather, road or traffic.

hooks_spoken: Read the center lines from your side: two solid means no pass, a broken line on your side means you may, two broken means either side may, and finish before the lines go solid.
Solid lines may be crossed carefully only to turn into or out of a driveway, and Safe Corridors highways carry doubled fines for speeding and aggressive driving.

hooks_spoken: Pass on the left; the right is allowed only with steady multi-lane traffic or a left-turning driver ahead with room, and the shoulder is never allowed.
Skip passing wherever you cannot see ahead, keep to the right half and the rightmost lane, and give way to sirens, flashing lights, trains, buses and postal vehicles.

hooks_spoken: Every corner of an intersection has a crosswalk, painted or not, and a pedestrian there gets a full stop until your lane and the next one are clear.
Keep stopping even after Don't Walk shows, never pass a car stopped for a walker, yield to mobility device users, and know that failing to stop brings fines, jail, suspension and points.

hooks_spoken: Stop behind the white line, tie at a multi-way stop goes to the right, a yield sign means slow and give way, a stop sign means stop close then yield, and a dark signal works as a four-way stop.
Never dodge a signal through private property; at an uncontrolled crossing slow down, the left vehicle yields to the right, driveway drivers yield to all, and circles follow their flow.

hooks_spoken: Join the highway at the speed of traffic, yield to the main road, never stop in the acceleration lane, and if you miss an exit just take the next one.
In a weave lane the exiting driver goes first; slow through cloverleafs and toll plazas, give disabled cars space, and if you break down pull over, flash, and stay locked inside.
